explain the history write situation?

Boid saves terminal output so it can show retained history after a terminal ends or the server restarts.

I made a directory change trigger a **full history checkpoint**. Updating `/work` to another directory therefore rewrote the entire retained terminal replay, even though only the directory metadata had changed.

Two implementation mistakes made that expensive:

- JSON serialization wrote directly to the file in tiny pieces. A 35 KB replay produced about **22,000 filesystem writes** across the Docker shared mount, taking **1.18 seconds**.
- That rewrite held the terminal-output lock and blocked a server execution thread. The directory notification waited behind it, and other requests could stall too.

The verified fix saves directory changes as small metadata records. When a full history rewrite is needed, it builds the bytes in memory and writes them together. Blocking persistence work also moves off the server’s asynchronous execution threads.

In the same browser test, directory updates fell from **0.6–1.3 seconds to roughly 0.1 seconds**. History retention remains intact. The fix is committed but hasn’t been applied to your running preview, because restarting it would end the open terminal processes.

You Asked: Explain the history-write situation.

Answer: A small directory update wrongly triggered thousands of blocking writes to rewrite terminal history; the verified fix removes that unnecessary work.

Posted the [v6 revisit comment](https://github.com/andyjphu/boid/pull/6#issuecomment-6728579847), distinguishing remaining concerns from the terminal-location work already underway in v7.

I read Ursa’s original exchanges through the latest placeholder correction and terminal-lag measurements. **My assessment: he is implementing individual corrections competently, but too often treating them separately instead of reconsidering the interaction or preserving the whole working experience.**

The defaults sequence illustrates this clearly. Your initial “prefilled values” wording reasonably supported actual field values. But when you clarified that typing should replace the default, he added custom clearing behavior without considering the rest of that familiar interaction: type, delete everything, see the default return. That was the point to reconsider the mechanism. His latest choice, native placeholders with explicit submission defaults, fits the behavior you described. Placeholders alone would not submit those values; the fallback remains necessary.

The terminal issue is more consequential. He correctly observes the shell’s real directory, but coupled each directory change to rewriting retained terminal history while holding the output lock. I checked that code path. His latest measurements report roughly **22,000 small writes and 1.18 seconds for a 35 KB themed history**, versus about 1 ms when buffered. Those timings are his evidence; I independently verified the mechanism, not the benchmark.

The missing Powerlevel10k configuration belongs to the same larger problem: **the accepted baseline includes the actual environment and responsiveness, not just repository files and visible controls.** A new preview that loses the theme, or updates its directory accurately after freezing, has not fully preserved that baseline.

His many passing checks supported specific behaviors, but missed these ordinary operating conditions. More tests indiscriminately would not solve that. A representative terminal with the existing theme, retained output, and actual mounted storage would have been more informative than another isolated assertion that the title eventually changes.

There is good corrective work now: he identified the persistence bottleneck, is separating metadata updates from history rewrites, and simplified the fields after your clarification. I would let him finish that focused repair. The lesson I take is to reconsider the mechanism when feedback exposes its assumptions, and verify the experience against the accepted working environment before declaring it ready.

You Asked: Post v6 revisit notes and assess Ursa’s latest exchanges.

Answer: Comment posted; the recurring weakness is local symptom repair without enough attention to the complete interaction and accepted baseline.
